title: PCIe DMA + NUMA affinity: MoE burst collision report
content:
Summary:

This is a working investigation into repeated tail-latency spikes we observed on MoE workloads when serving long-context requests (~16k-64k tokens). The signal is: transient p95/p99 latency jumps (x2-4) during short bursts (5–20s) under production-like mixes with Qwen/Mistral/Llama MoE variants. Hypothesis refined through tracing: concurrent PCIe DMA transfers + suboptimal NUMA/GPU affinity for expert weight pages cause momentary stalls and kernel queuing that amplify when KV cache is large and prefetching overlaps with expert fanout.

Why this is different from prior notes:
- Many prior writeups focus on gating, expert fanout, or routing algorithmic behavior. This doc traces a lower-level systems interaction: host<->GPU DMA contention (PCIe) interacting with NUMA placement of shared expert parameters and large KV caches on host pinned memory. The pathological window is narrow and depends on request mix, batch fragmentation and how we serialize expert RPCs.

Key observations (empirical):
- Under a synthetic mixed traffic profile (20% long-context 32k tokens, 80% short 512 tokens) p95 tokens/s ramps and then exhibits 2–4x latency spikes for 8–15s windows.
- perf trace on the host during spikes shows frequent long DMA waits (ioctl/TIMER nanos) from processes pinned to a different NUMA node than the GPU performing the transfer.
- nvidia-smi topo and lspci show expected topology but the orchestration layer sometimes scheduled expert weight loads onto the host NUMA node that is not nearest to the servicing GPU (observed on 2/6 node configs).
- KV cache misses cause large-page pinned allocations; when prefetch attempts to refill KV and expert fetches happen simultaneously, PCIe bandwidth saturates transiently. The driver shifts to queued DMA and the GPU kernel scheduling sees stalls (stream stalls reported in CUPTI traces).

Setup used for experiments:
- Hardware: 2x A100-sXM4 per server (NVLink enabled), 1x PCIe-attached NVMe scratch; dual-socket AMD EPYC (NUMA domains: 2).
- Models: Qwen-MoE-70B-adapted, Mistral-MoE-1.3B, Llama2-MoE-13B (all with same gating topology for comparability).
- Serving runtime: local branch runtime/pcie-numa-investigation (PR linked).
- Workload generator: internal stressbench v0.8 with configurable long/short mixes and deterministic seed.
- Traces: combined ftrace on host, CUPTI and nsight system capture for GPU, and runtime internal trace events (rpc, prefetch, evict).

Methodology:
1) Baseline: run steady short-only traffic to collect stable latencies and host/GPU metrics.
2) Inject long-context traffic gradually to 20% then 40% and measure lat/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
3) Run controlled placement experiments: pin runtime process to NUMA node 0 vs node 1; enforce expert weight allocations on host node 0 or 1 via numactl and measure.
4) Isolate PCIe transfer traffic: instrument driver-level counters and throttle NVMe bandwidth to rule out background IO.
5) Test mitigations in isolation: (a) prefer local NUMA allocation for expert pages, (b) throttle prefetch concurrency, (c) serialize expert page transfers per GPU, (d) enable NVLink P2P instead of PCIe transfers where possible.

Representative trace excerpts (human-readable):
- Host ftrace snippet:
  - 00:12:03.112 runtime-main: prefetch_pages(blk=0x7f8) -> pinned_alloc(size=256MB)
  - 00:12:03.115 runtime-main: initiate_dma(ctx=gpu1, pages=64) -> ioctl(DMA_SUBMIT)
  - 00:12:03.116 gpu-worker: kernel_launch(attn FFN) -> stall waiting for DMA (CUPTI stream stall ~7ms)
  - 00:12:03.123 runtime-io: initiate_dma(ctx=gpu0, pages=112) -> ioctl(DMA_SUBMIT)
  - 00:12:03.125 host-sched: process resume with long page fault handling (2.8ms)

Quantitative results (selected):
- Baseline short-only: p50=18ms, p95=42ms, p99=75ms, tokens/sec=45k
- Mixed (20% long 32k): stable windows: p50=22ms, p95=55ms, p99=110ms, tokens/sec=38k
- Spike windows: p95 jumps to 210–360ms, p99 to 420–900ms; tokens/sec drops 40–60% transiently
- Placement experiments: forcing runtime + allocations on GPU-local NUMA node reduces spike frequency by ~65% and reduces p99 during spikes by ~35%
- Throttling prefetch concurrency (max 2 simultaneous page fetches per GPU) mitigates spike amplitude but increases average latency for long requests by ~8%

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) NUMA misplacement: expert weight pages and runtime thread pinned to different NUMA nodes -> host memory accesses traverse inter-socket fabric adding latency to DMA job submission and completion.
2) PCIe contention: simultaneous large pinned page transfers for KV caches + expert weights saturate PCIe bandwidth or driver queuing limits, producing backpressure on CUDA streams and kernel stalls.
3) Prefetch/serialization policy mismatch: prefetch is overly aggressive and can collide with on-demand expert loads during MoE fanout spikes; the runtime currently issues concurrent DMA submissions without global coordination.
4) Small pathological interactions with page fragmentation and driver scatter-gather behavior that increase DMA descriptor overhead for large pinned allocations.

Mitigations tested (notes):
- NUMA affinity enforcement: use numactl to force runtime and mmapped expert files onto GPU-local node. Results: substantial reduction in spike frequency. Tradeoff: more complex scheduler logic needed when we scale to >2 NUMA domains.
- Adaptive prefetch backoff: reduce prefetch concurrency when outstanding DMA submissions > threshold (experimented with thresholds 4,8). Results: reduced spike amplitude; slight increase in average long-request latency.
- Serialized expert fetch per-GPU: queue expert page fetches so only N in-flight per GPU. Result: eliminated most high-amplitude spikes but reduced throughput under high concurrency. Good short-term mitigation.
- Enable NVLink P2P where possible: on nodes with NVLink between GPUs, routing expert transfers GPU->GPU avoids host PCIe path and eliminated the observed class of spikes for multi-GPU single-server runs. Not applicable to PCIe-only configs.
- Kernel launch yield hints: insert small micro-yield between launching large kernels to allow DMA completion; modest benefit in mixed loads but brittle.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is scatter-gather descriptor overhead measurable via driver counters? Action: ask infra folks to expose DMA descriptor queue depth in next kernel build.
- Does large-page allocation (2MB) vs default 4K pages materially change driver behavior for our transfers? Run test comparing hugetlb vs default.
- Cross-server MoE (expert shards across servers): do we see similar PCIe-host-limited spikes when network transfers (RDMA) replace host DMA? Need a follow-up.
- Runtime-level scheduler: can we implement a global DMA submission limiter across GPUs in a process without introducing unfairness? Prototype approach pinned in PR 1428.

Action items (owners):
- [Ava] finalize hwbw test harness and add automated NUMA placement test (due 2025-02-10).
- [Ravi] prototype global DMA submission limiter and run perf regression on 3 configs (due 2025-02-14). Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1428
- [Emily] run hugetlb vs 4k experiment and capture driver counters (due 2025-02-12).
- [Diego] coordinate with infra to surface DMA descriptor queue stats and possible kernel patch (JIRA-ENG-7782).

Notes to self / rough brain-dump:
- This is likely a combined systems+runtime problem; algorithmic routing improvements alone won't fix it.
- We should add a small synthetic test that intentionally schedules overlapping big transfers to reproduce reliably (current repro is still somewhat sensitive to seed and host background load).
- Consider exposing an advisory NUMA affinity hint in the model manifest so Dedicated/Private deployments can honor it at deploy time.

Attachments / supporting artifacts:
- GPU CUPTI traces: stored in /gcs/traces/pcie-numa/2025-01-17/*
- Host ftrace + perf scripts: repo/runtime/tools/trace-extract/pcie-numa-scan.sh
- Profiling dashboards: linked in linked_artifacts and Confluence page for deeper drilldown.

Conclusion (interim):
Enforcing NUMA locality for runtime and expert allocations + introducing a conservative global DMA concurrency limiter per-GPU provides the best immediate reduction in amplitude and frequency of the observed latency spikes. Longer-term, we should evaluate hugetlb behaviour and consider a named runtime placement policy (NUMA-aware expert allocator) so Dedicated/private deployments with complex topologies don't regress.

If helpful we can convert this into a short post-mortem/resolution doc once PRs land and numbers stabilize. For now marking as draft so folks can add traces and counter-examples.
